title: Working Scientifically
seo_title: Year 5 Science: Working Scientifically Worksheets (Variables, Fair Tests, Means)
standard_text: Plan different types of scientific enquiries to answer questions, including recognising and controlling variables where necessary; take measurements with increasing accuracy and precision, taking repeat readings when appropriate; record data and results using tables, bar and line graphs; use test results to make predictions to set up further comparative and fair tests; report and present findings, including conclusions.
meta_desc: Free Year 5 science worksheets on working scientifically: variables in Year 5 investigations, fair tests, repeat readings, means, graphs, predictions and conclusions. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Plan it fairly, measure it carefully.
key_sub: Change one thing, measure one thing, repeat and let the results decide.
body_html:
How to think about it

A fair test changes one variable, measures one variable and keeps the rest the same.

  • Plan: question, prediction, variables, equipment.
  • Measure carefully; repeat readings; spot anomalous results; find the mean.
  • Show results in a table and the right graph; write a conclusion that the evidence supports.
Example

Parachute size and fall time: what do you change?

The question names it

Answer: the size of the parachute

Example

Times 3.1, 3.3, 3.2 s. Mean?

(3.1 + 3.3 + 3.2) ÷ 3

Answer: 3.2 s

Common mistakes

  • Changing two things at once.
  • Doing a test only once.
  • Writing a conclusion that goes further than the results.

faq.a: Only one variable is changed, one is measured, and all the others are kept the same.
To check our results, spot anomalous ones and work out a more reliable mean.

faq.q: How do I write a conclusion?
faq.a: Say what the results show, answer the question you asked, and only claim what the evidence supports.

items.q: Why is a fair test important?
c: so you know the change you made caused the result
so the result is what you predicted
so everyone gets the same mark
items.e: Only one thing changes.

items.q: Which variable do you measure?
items.e: It is the result.

items.q: Investigation: "Does the size of a parachute affect how long it takes to fall?" What should be measured?
c: the same load, the same material and the same drop height
items.e: Measure the result (the dependent variable).

items.q: Investigation: "Does stirring affect how fast sugar dissolves?" Which variable should be changed?
c: the same amount of sugar and water at the same temperature
the time for the sugar to dissolve
how much the water is stirred
items.e: Change one variable: the one in the question.

items.q: Investigation: "Does the number of spoons of bicarbonate of soda affect how much a balloon inflates?" What should be kept the same to make it a fair test?
c: the same amount of vinegar and the same size of bottle and balloon
the number of spoons of bicarbonate of soda
items.e: Control variables keep the test fair.

items.q: Which variable do you change on purpose?
items.e: It goes in the first column of a table.

items.q: Investigation: "Does the shape of plasticine affect how fast it sinks in water?" What should be kept the same to make it a fair test?
c: the same mass of plasticine and the same tube of water
items.e: Control variables keep the test fair.

items.q: Investigation: "Does the type of surface affect how far a toy car rolls?" Which variable should be changed?
c: the same car, the same ramp height and letting go without pushing
items.e: Change one variable: the one in the question.

items.q: What is a variable in an investigation?
c: something that can change or be changed
items.e: Change one, measure one, control the rest.

items.q: Why should measurements be read at eye level?
items.e: Avoid reading at an angle.
